# Session Begin

The first command of a session — the mirror image of `/session-end`. Session-end wrote
everything worth keeping to disk before the last session ended; session-begin reads
it back so this session starts as smart as the last one finished. The output
is a short briefing, not a report: what we understand, what's ready to do, and
a suggested starting point.

Everything here is read-only. Session-begin never modifies files, claims issues, or
starts work on its own — it ends with the agent oriented and awaiting (or
confirming) direction.

## The flow

### 1 — Locate the project

Work from the project root: the git root if inside a repository, otherwise the
current working directory. If the directory is clearly not a project (e.g., a
home directory with no repo), say so and ask which project to wake up in.

### 2 — Read the reflections

Read `.claude/REFLECTIONS.md` at the project root — the whole file; it is
deliberately kept short enough to read cold. This is the reflective memory
`/session-end` maintains: current understanding, lessons and gotchas, failed
approaches, open questions. It exists precisely for this moment, so don't skim
it — the gotchas and dead ends are what stop this session from repeating the
last one's mistakes.

If the file doesn't exist, note that briefly (one line, not an apology) and
move on. Don't go hunting for substitutes in other memory files — CLAUDE.md is
already loaded by the harness, and git history is available if needed later.

### 3 — Check the Beads backlog

Beads is configured when the project root has a `.beads/` directory. If it
doesn't, skip this step **silently** — don't mention Beads, `bd`, or the
absence of a backlog anywhere in the briefing. The user asked to be caught up
on their project, not for an inventory of tooling it doesn't use; "no backlog
to check" is noise wearing the costume of information.

When Beads is configured, do two things:

**Find the ready work** — open issues with no blockers:

- Prefer the `/beads:ready` skill (invoke `beads:ready` via the Skill tool) if
  it's in your available-skills list — it uses the Beads MCP tools and handles
  presentation and claiming.
- Otherwise run `bd ready` directly. If it returns nothing, check `bd list
  --status in_progress` and `bd blocked` — an empty ready list with
  in-progress or blocked issues is a different situation than an empty
  backlog, and the briefing should say which.

**Read the handoff** — always, not just when the issues look thin. Session-end
leaves handoff notes via `bd remember`, and they carry exactly what issue
titles can't: design decisions already made, the file to start in, the trap
the last session already stepped around. Run `bd memories` to list stored
memories and `bd recall <key>` on anything that reads like a handoff or
touches the ready work (the previews truncate — recall the full content
before relying on it). Skipping this is how a session re-decides something
that was settled yesterday.

### 4 — Brief and hand over

End with one compact briefing — a few lines per section, only sections that
have content:

- **Where we are** — two or three sentences of current understanding from
  REFLECTIONS.md, plus any gotcha or open question likely to matter today.
- **Ready work** — the ready issues (id, title, priority), or the honest state
  of the backlog (all blocked, something already in progress, empty). Weave in
  what the handoff memory settled — "design is fetch-then-merge, start in
  engine.go" changes how the first hour goes.
- **Suggested start** — one concrete recommendation: usually the highest
  priority ready issue, or the open question blocking everything else.

Then stop and let the user direct — or, if the user already said what they
want ("wake up and get going on the next thing"), proceed straight into the
suggested start. Don't pad the briefing with restated file contents; the value
is selection, not coverage.

# Project Reflections

Reflective notes maintained at session wrap-up. Rules to obey live in
`CLAUDE.md`; backlog and work state live in Beads (`bd`); the authoritative
design intent lives in `docs/SPEC.md` + the ADRs. This file is for
*understanding* — mental models, gotchas-with-context, and why decisions went
the way they did — the kind of thing that has no natural home in an issue
tracker.

## Current understanding

- **Top-level Slack messages already reach the daemon; thread-only scope is a
  choice, not a technical limit.** With `channels:history` + the
  `message.channels` Event Subscription, Slack delivers *every* channel message
  to the `message` handler in `src/slack/inbound-router.ts` — including
  top-level ones that @mention the bot. The router drops them only because they
  lack a `thread_ts`. Consequence: supporting top-level @mentions would **not**
  require the `app_mentions:read` scope / an `app_mention` handler (the natural
  assumption, and the one bd `meal-planner-kqq` was written under). A dedicated
  `app_mention` path would be *cleaner*, but the message event is already in
  hand. We deliberately kept thread-only anyway (SPEC §7; ratified in bd
  `meal-planner-j8b`) because the whole revision loop keys on `thread_ts →
  session row`, so a top-level message has no plan context to act on. Read the
  RUNBOOK's "does nothing, by design" line with this nuance: *by design*, not
  *impossible*.

- **The planner had literal amnesia until 2026-09-27, and it showed.** Dedup
  depends on the Todoist recency read, which failed every week (bd `54i`) and
  whose data source (the v3.0 round-trip, `4sr`) isn't live — so across 7
  weeks of plans the bot used only **17 distinct recipes out of 765**. The fix
  (bd `5uy`, PR #75) treats each week's *initial* posted plan as accepted:
  `session.initial_plan` is written once at suggest and never revised, and
  `plan-memory.ts` unions the last 8 weeks' main dishes with the Todoist read.
  Two design choices worth keeping in mind: (1) *initial*, not latest — the
  user's explicit call, and `working_plan`/`last_posted_plan` both mutate on
  revision, hence the new column; (2) the union catches a Todoist throw
  *itself*, because `buildPlan`'s degrade-silently catch would otherwise
  discard the local memory along with the failed Todoist result.

## Lessons & gotchas

- **Model dependency edges from the durable work, not toward closed work.**
  When a bead is a *stopgap that exists only until some real work lands*, the
  blocking edge points **real-work → stopgap** (the real work blocks the
  stopgap, because finishing it makes the stopgap unnecessary). Example this
  backlog: `4sr` (v3.0 round-trip go-live) **blocks** `88j` (interim recency
  back-fill CLI) — once the prod round-trip is live and writing recency data,
  `88j` is moot. Corollary: never wire a `blocks` edge against an
  already-**closed** bead — it would assert open work is waiting on something
  finished. Use a `relates_to` link instead for context to closed beads (e.g.
  `88j ↔ v9v`/`chj`: the dedup epic + the ADR-0006 decision that named the
  v2.0/v3.0 phase-ordering hole `88j` bridges).

- **A routine `brew upgrade` took prod down for ~3 weeks by replacing the
  daemon's `node` and `op` binaries — three distinct failure modes, one trigger**
  (2026-08-19 incident, bd `meal-planner-93k`; my *first* diagnosis here blamed
  an ekreader cert rotation and was wrong — recorded so the mistake isn't
  repeated). On **Aug 1** `brew` bumped `node` 26.5.0 → 26.5.1 (**deleting** the
  26.5.0 binary) and `1password-cli`, near the macOS 26.5.2 upgrade. That one
  event caused, in sequence:
  1. **Ghost-binary TCC failure.** The daemon had run since Jul 26 on node
     26.5.0; after Aug 1 that process held a binary no longer on disk. macOS TCC
     can't validate a deleted binary, so the daemon's calendar (`ekreader`, exit
     3) and Notes (`osascript -1743`) reads began failing on the next weekly run
     (Aug 2). **This was the "calendar failing" symptom — not the ekreader
     grant.** ekreader reads the calendar fine (verified 20 real events); its
     grant was never broken. A running daemon can silently rot the moment
     `brew` deletes the binary underneath it, while `git`/`ps` look normal.
  2. **Gatekeeper block on the fresh binaries.** Restarting to clear the ghost
     surfaced that the freshly-installed, *quarantined* node 26.5.1 and op were
     blocked by macOS `AppleSystemPolicy` ("Security policy would not allow
     process"). `op` hung spawning its `op-daemon` child (all threads parked in
     `__psynch_cvwait`, zero output), so secrets-load timed out at 15s and the
     daemon crash-looped. **Fix: approve *both* `op` and `node` in Privacy &
     Security** — the launchd daemon's own main binary (`node`) needs approval,
     not just the tool it shells out to. This op breakage was latent since ~Aug
     1: the daemon would have died on *any* reboot regardless; the restart
     merely surfaced it.
  3. **Voided per-binary TCC grants.** TCC keys Automation/Calendar grants to
     the exact Cellar path/cdhash, so node 26.5.1 inherits none of node
     26.5.0's grants. node 26.5.1 lacked Full Disk Access until
     2026-09-27 (`notes-tags: could not open NoteStore … unable to open
     database file` every run; only the tag refresh was skipped). FDA is now
     granted (TCC.db `auth_value=2`); the Oct 4 run is the first real proof.
  **Prevention now in place:** `brew pin node` + `brew pin 1password-cli` so a
  background `brew upgrade` can't silently replace them again. Diagnostic
  reflex for "op hangs": `sample <pid>` a stuck process (no sudo needed) and
  grep the system log for `AppleSystemPolicy` — that's what pinned it to
  Gatekeeper. And note the failure was *invisible from the outside*: the daemon
  kept posting a degraded (static all-FULL, no-dedup) plan and only the alert
  log showed it — read `logs/meal-planner.err.log`, don't trust "it still
  posted."

- **An unanswerable consent prompt + a fatal boot timeout + `KeepAlive` = a
  prompt flood** (2026-09-23, just before the macOS 27.0 upgrade; bd
  `meal-planner-dx2`). `op read` blocked on a macOS dialog; the dialog said
  "node" because TCC names the *responsible* process (launchd → node → op).
  The 15s secrets timeout exited the process, `KeepAlive` relaunched it at
  once, and each new process raised a fresh "Allow" prompt — endless dialogs
  until the user set `KeepAlive=false` by hand. The likely source is `op`
  probing the 1Password desktop app (installed; its group container is
  `2BUA8C4S2C.com.1password`) even though a service-account token needs no
  app integration. `OP_BIOMETRIC_UNLOCK_ENABLED=false` in the plist env
  (PR #73) made the next boot load secrets cleanly — consistent with, not
  proof of, that cause (the system log had already rotated). In hindsight the
  August "op hangs, all threads parked in `__psynch_cvwait`" symptom is the
  same shape: a process waiting on a dialog. Treat any headless `op` hang as
  "who is it waiting on?" before blaming the network.

- **Bead state no longer touches git (2026-09-27, PRs #77 + `37e8979`).** Both
  `.beads/issues.jsonl` and `.beads/interactions.jsonl` are gitignored. The
  tracked export was the source of constant tree churn — every claim, comment,
  or close forced a beads-only commit or a direct push to `main` — and of the
  July "discarded real statuses via `git checkout --`" incident; untracking
  removes both. Bead state rides `refs/dolt/data` (`bd dolt push`). Caveat:
  `interactions.jsonl` is bd's optional audit sidecar, **not** in Dolt, so its
  entries after 2026-09-27 exist only on this Mac.

- **Don't verify with real writes against the live tracker.** A "does a bd
  write leave the tree clean?" check was done with `bd comments add ...
  test-noise` on a real bead (54i) — and embedded-mode bd has no comment
  delete (`bd sql` is unsupported there), so the noise is permanent. Use a
  read-only check or a throwaway bead you can close.

- **A handoff's "lead" is a hypothesis, not a diagnosis — 54i proved it.**
  The recorded lead for "Todoist recency: Invalid argument value" was
  `toISOString` millisecond precision; a read-only live repro disproved it in
  minutes (ms precision returns 200). The real cause was the live plist's
  `MP_TODOIST_PROJECT_ID_PROD` holding a **pre-2025 numeric Todoist project
  id**, which the v1 API rejects (`error_extra.argument: "project_id"`); the
  RUNBOOK had told us to source it from the deprecated v2 endpoint. Two
  takeaways: the error body *named the field* all along but our client threw
  it away (PR #79 now folds `error_extra.argument` into the message), and a
  config-value bug survives every rebuild — "persists across builds" pointed
  at env, not code. Fixed in prod 2026-09-29 (`6Crcx82JRXcwQQv3`); the Oct 4
  run is the proof. Next layer down (bd `ww2`): completed meal tasks carry no
  `mp:rid=` marker, so recency will still resolve zero recipe ids.

- **Restart safety is back on (2026-09-29).** The Sep 23 lockdown had set
  `KeepAlive` *and* `RunAtLoad` false (so unload/load left the daemon
  stopped). `dx2` (PR #78) added a secrets-free boot-failure guard —
  persisted streak in `data/boot-failure-state.json`, one log alert per 30
  min, exponential backoff to 60s before `exit(1)` — and both flags were
  restored. The guard alerts to the local log only (no Slack: secrets may be
  what failed), so a boot crash-loop still shows up only in
  `logs/meal-planner.err.log`.

## Open questions

- **What happens to the plan memory once Todoist round-trip feedback flows?**
  Today it's a union: "recommended" and "actually completed" both count as
  recent. Once `4sr` is live, a recommended-but-rejected meal arguably
  shouldn't be excluded for 8 weeks — the user said this behavior will be
  "modified later to incorporate round-trip feedback," not yet designed.

- **`4sr` (round-trip go-live) is ops-only, not agent-drivable end-to-end.**
  It's 1Password secret storage, Slack-dashboard config (Event Subscriptions +
  slash-command registration), launchd reload, and TCC/prod verification on the
  family Mac — steps an agent can prep and sanity-check but can't execute
  headlessly. If splitting it later, the RUNBOOK §8.2 checklist maps cleanly
  onto sub-issues (secrets / Slack-config / the three live verifications:
  socket-opened, in-thread revision, `/mp-approve` commit).

# 🚨 SESSION CLOSE PROTOCOL 🚨

**CRITICAL**: Before saying "done" or "complete", you MUST run this checklist:

```
[ ] 1. bd close <id1> <id2> ...   (close completed issues)
[ ] 2. run quality gates        (tests, linters, builds when relevant)
[ ] 3. git status               (check what changed)
[ ] 4. follow active profile    (conservative: report handoff; team-maintainer: commit/sync/push if enabled)
```

**Policy:** Conservative is the default. Commit, sync, or push only when the active user, orchestrator, or repository profile grants that authority.

## Core Rules
- **Default**: Use beads for ALL task tracking (`bd create`, `bd ready`, `bd close`)
- **Prohibited**: Do NOT use TodoWrite, TaskCreate, or markdown files for task tracking
- **Workflow**: Create beads issue BEFORE writing code, mark in_progress when starting
- **Memory**: Use `bd remember "insight"` for persistent knowledge across sessions. Do NOT use MEMORY.md files — they fragment across accounts. Search with `bd memories <keyword>`.
- Persistence you don't need beats lost context
- Default: do not commit, push, or run dolt remote sync without explicit authority. Team-maintainer behavior is opt-in and still subordinate to user/orchestrator instructions.
- Git workflow: conservative by default; commit/push only with explicit user/orchestrator or team-maintainer authority
- Session management: check `bd ready` for available work

## Essential Commands

### Finding Work
- `bd ready` - Show issues ready to work (no blockers)
- `bd list --status=open` - All open issues
- `bd list --status=in_progress` - Your active work
- `bd show <id>` - Detailed issue view with dependencies

### Creating & Updating
- `bd create --title="Summary of this issue" --description="Why this issue exists and what needs to be done" --type=task|bug|feature --priority=2` - New issue
  - Priority: 0-4 or P0-P4 (0=critical, 2=medium, 4=backlog). NOT "high"/"medium"/"low"
- `bd create ... --parent=<id>` - Hierarchical child (task under epic, subtask under task; inherits parent labels)
- `bd update <id> --claim` - Claim work
- `bd unclaim <id>` - Release stuck issue (agent crashed)
- `bd update <id> --assignee=username` - Assign to someone
- `bd update <id> --if-assignee=<expected> --assignee=<new>` - Atomic reassign: applies only if the assignee still matches (--if-status=<expected> guards status; --if-assignee='' requires unassigned). Mismatch exits non-zero with nothing written — never retry blindly
- `bd update <id> --title/--description/--notes/--design` - Update fields inline
- `bd close <id>` - Mark complete
- `bd close <id1> <id2> ...` - Close multiple issues at once (more efficient)
- `bd close <id> --reason="explanation"` - Close with reason
- **Tip**: When creating multiple issues/tasks/epics, use parallel subagents for efficiency
- **WARNING**: Do NOT use `bd edit` - it opens $EDITOR (vim/nano) which blocks agents

### Dependencies & Blocking
- `bd dep add <issue> <depends-on>` - Add dependency (issue depends on depends-on)
- `bd blocked` - Show all blocked issues
- `bd show <id>` - See what's blocking/blocked by this issue

### Sync & Collaboration
- `bd dolt push` - Push beads to Dolt remote
- `bd dolt pull` - Pull beads from Dolt remote
- `bd search <query>` - Search issues by keyword

### Project Health
- `bd stats` - Project statistics (open/closed/blocked counts)
- `bd doctor` - Check for issues (sync problems, missing hooks)
- `bd doctor --check=conventions` - Check for convention drift (lint, stale, orphans)

### Quality Tools
- `bd create --validate` - Check description has required sections
- `bd create --acceptance="criteria"` - Set acceptance criteria (checked by --validate)
- `bd create --design="decisions"` - Record design decisions
- `bd create --notes="context"` - Add supplementary notes
- `bd config set validation.on-create warn` - Auto-validate on every create
- `bd lint` - Check existing issues for missing sections

### Lifecycle & Hygiene
- `bd defer <id> --until="date"` - Defer work to a future date
- `bd supersede <id> --with=<new-id>` - Mark issue as superseded
- `bd close <id> --suggest-next` - Show newly unblocked issues after closing
- `bd stale` - Find issues with no recent activity
- `bd orphans` - Find issues with broken dependencies
- `bd preflight` - Pre-PR checks (lint, stale, orphans)
- `bd human <id>` - Flag for human decision (list/respond/dismiss)

### Structured Workflows
- `bd formula list` - See available workflow templates
- `bd mol pour <name>` - Start structured workflow from formula

**Starting work:**
```bash
bd ready           # Find available work
bd show <id>       # Review issue details
bd update <id> --claim  # Claim it
```

**Completing work:**
```bash
bd close <id1> <id2> ...    # Close all completed issues at once
git status                  # Check changed files

### 0.1 macOS permissions (TCC) — grant before first run

Reading Apple Notes needs two separate macOS **TCC** (Transparency, Consent &
Control) grants, applied to **the process that runs the daemon** — the `node`
binary launchd executes (from `which node`; see §7), or your terminal app when
you run `pnpm sync` / `pnpm dev` by hand:

1. **Automation → Notes** — `osascript`/JXA controlling Notes.app (how
   `readNotes` reads note bodies). System Settings → **Privacy & Security →
   Automation** → find the daemon's app/binary → enable the **Notes** toggle.
2. **Full Disk Access** — reading `NoteStore.sqlite` directly (how the NoteStore
   hashtag read works, `q95.13`). System Settings → **Privacy & Security → Full
   Disk Access** → **＋** → add the daemon's `node` binary (⌘⇧G to type the
   absolute path) → enable its toggle.
3. **Calendars** (v2.0+, only if `calendar.enabled=true`) — the compiled
   **native EventKit** helper (`native/ekreader`, built by `pnpm build:native`;
   how `readCalendarEvents`, `src/calendar/calendar-reader.ts`, reads events
   for ADR-0004's calendar capacity classification; bead ob8 replaced the
   original `osascript`/JXA backend). This grant targets **`native/ekreader`
   itself, not the daemon's `node` binary**. To grant it, **run the binary
   once from a foreground session** — `native/ekreader "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)"
   "$(date -u -v+7d +%FT%TZ)" "Family Schedule" "Appointments"` — which raises
   the "…would like to access your Calendars" prompt (its embedded
   `Info.plist` `NSCalendarsFullAccessUsageDescription` is what makes a bare
   CLI promptable at all — without it macOS auto-denies silently); click
   **Allow**. It then prints the events as JSON. (It will also appear under
   System Settings → **Privacy & Security → Calendars** where it can be
   toggled, but the run-once prompt is the reliable trigger for a bare binary.)
   **The grant carries to the headless launchd daemon** and **survives
   rebuilds**: `pnpm build:native` signs the binary with a stable Apple
   Development certificate (`--identifier com.backhaus.meal-planner.ekreader`,
   overridable via `MP_EKREADER_SIGN_IDENTITY`), so TCC keys on the stable
   designated requirement (identifier + team), not a per-build ad-hoc hash —
   **no re-grant after a recompile** (verified 2026-07-25: bead ob8/12p — grant
   granted once interactively then read the live calendar under a launchd
   LaunchAgent, both direct-exec and via `node`). Node itself needs no
   Calendars grant.
   Degrade-safe: with `calendar.enabled=false` (the default) or an
   ungranted/failed read (native EventKit denies **fast**, no hang), the
   daemon falls back to the static v1.0 cook-night count and alerts
   `#agent-alerts` once (ADR-0004 D6) — it never fails the Sunday post, so
   this grant is only needed once you opt a deployment into the v2.0 calendar
   feature.

**Why this must happen before/at first run, not lazily:** the very first
`osascript` Notes access raises a **one-time permission dialog**, and **launchd
has no UI to answer it** — under launchd the prompt cannot be shown, so the read
either silently returns nothing or the blocked dialog **hangs `osascript`**
(a hang vector for the trigger watchdog, `bd6.11`; the read is also bounded by
`notes-reader`'s `READ_TIMEOUT_MS`). Trigger and answer the prompt **once in the
foreground first** so the grant is recorded before launchd ever runs:

```bash
# From the checkout, with config/secrets in the env (§3–§4). Answer "OK" when
# macOS prompts to let the terminal/node control Notes, then confirm rows exist.
pnpm sync
```

If the daemon runs under a **different** binary path than the terminal you
grant here (launchd uses `which node`'s absolute path, not your shell), grant
that exact binary too — TCC keys on the binary/bundle identity, so a new path
is an ungranted path.

### 0.2 Re-verify after every macOS update

**A macOS upgrade can reset or drop these TCC grants**, and a **new node binary
path** (a Homebrew/`nvm` upgrade that moves `node`) reads as a brand-new,
ungranted process. Either turns the next weekly sync into a **silent or hanging
no-op** with the daemon otherwise looking healthy. After any OS update (or node
upgrade), **re-verify before trusting the next Sunday**:

```bash
pnpm sync            # should read your recipe corpus and print total>0
```

- If it **reads 0 notes while the index already holds recipes**, the daemon now
  **alerts loudly** to `#agent-alerts` + the local log (proceed + alert,
  `fkg.7`) instead of silently planning against a stale index — treat that alert
  as "re-check Automation + Full Disk Access", not "the corpus is empty".
- Re-confirm both toggles in System Settings are still enabled for the daemon's
  current `node` binary; re-run the foreground `pnpm sync` to re-trigger the
  prompt if a grant was dropped.
- If `calendar.enabled=true` (v2.0+), the **Calendars** grant from §0.1 item 3
  (on `native/ekreader`, not `node`) can still be dropped by an **OS upgrade** —
  a dropped grant degrades to the static cook-night count + a one-time
  `#agent-alerts` alert (ADR-0004 D6) rather than a hang or failed post; re-grant
  by re-triggering the prompt in the foreground (run the binary once, §0.1 item
  3). A `pnpm build:native` recompile does **not** drop it — the stable-cert
  signature keeps the same designated requirement across rebuilds (bead ob8/12p).

Stop the walkthrough for a moment: there's a bigger problem than the grants. **The node binary prod runs can no longer start.** Your Homebrew upgrade at 15:42 today replaced two libraries node depends on, `simdjson` (5.0.4 → 5.2.0) and `simdutf` (→ 9.4.0). Node itself is pinned at 26.11.1, so it still expects the old library files, and those were deleted.

- **The daemon still works for now.** PID 1471 loaded the old library before it was deleted and still has it in memory.
- **Any restart or reboot will crash-loop it.** Node fails before any of our code runs, so the boot-failure guard can't step in. Every `pnpm` command is broken right now too.
- **The pin itself caused this.** `brew pin node` freezes node but not the libraries it uses.

I've added this to `uzt`. The fix is to move to a node that matches the current libraries (26.13.1). Its new path gets new grants anyway, so the grant steps just shift to it. Run these one at a time:

```
! HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 brew unpin node
```
```
! HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 brew upgrade node
```

Then I'll check that the new node starts and that the native modules (`better-sqlite3`) still load. After that:
- Full Disk Access and Automation→Notes for the new Cellar path.
- Gatekeeper approval, if macOS blocks the new binary like it did in August.
- `brew pin 1password-cli`.
- A daemon restart, which you'll run.

**Decision for later:** pinning a Homebrew node is now proven to break prod, and not pinning means grants break on every upgrade. One option is to run prod on the official nodejs.org installer at `/usr/local/bin/node`. It's self-contained and Homebrew never touches it, so grants only need redoing when you upgrade it on purpose. I'd recommend it, but it changes the plist's `ProgramArguments`, so it's your call.

Node is unpinned. Next, the upgrade. It downloads and installs node 26.13.1, so it may take a minute:

```
! HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE=1 brew upgrade node
```

After that I'll check that it starts and that the native modules load. The running daemon keeps working while it runs.

content.text:
Short version: you update it by hand, on your schedule. The one real coupling it adds is between the node that runs prod and the node that `pnpm install` uses in your shell.

**Keeping it updated**
- The nodejs.org installer doesn't auto-update. You download the new `.pkg` and run it, or script `curl` → check against `SHASUMS256.txt` → `sudo installer -pkg`.
- For a local daemon that only makes outbound calls (Slack, Anthropic, Todoist), I'd pick an LTS line and upgrade quarterly or when a security release comes out. Each upgrade ends with the launchd test job and a daemon restart, which is today's checklist minus the dylib surprise.
- The upside, which I haven't verified: I believe the official binary is signed with the Node.js Foundation's Developer ID. If so, macOS ties grants to that signing identity rather than to the exact file, so they should survive upgrades. Homebrew's node is only ad-hoc signed (the system log showed that today), which is why every Homebrew upgrade drops the grants.
- To check after installing: `codesign -dv /usr/local/bin/node` should show a `TeamIdentifier`. Then rerun the test job after the first upgrade.

**Dependencies between versions.** I checked the code and nothing besides the main process depends on node:
- The daemon starts no child `node` processes. Notes reading is `osascript`, calendar is `ekreader`, secrets are `op`.
- The Agent SDK (0.3.206) runs its own bundled `darwin-arm64` binary, not node.

So the only coupling is **native modules**:
- `better-sqlite3` and `sqlite-vec` are compiled for one node *major* version (today's `process.versions.modules` = 147).
- Prod runs from this checkout's `node_modules`, and `pnpm install`/`rebuild` compiles them with whatever `node` is first on **your shell's** PATH.
- If your shell's Homebrew node moves to a new major while prod stays on its own install, the next `pnpm install` builds modules prod can't load. The daemon then fails at boot with a `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` mismatch.
- Patch and minor upgrades are safe. Only a major-version change breaks this.

**Ways to handle that coupling:**
1. **Use one node for both** (simplest). Uninstall Homebrew's node and use the official one for dev and prod. Homebrew packages that depend on node (check with `brew uses --installed node`) would pull it back in.
2. **Separate prod from dev.** Keep a dedicated prod checkout (a worktree or second clone) where you build with the prod node: `PATH=/usr/local/bin:$PATH pnpm install && pnpm build`. Your dev checkout can then use any node, and the plist points at the prod checkout. That's full separation, but deploying becomes "pull and build in the prod checkout."
3. **Guard rail, works with either.** Add `engines.node` in `package.json`, plus a boot-time check that fails loudly when the running ABI differs from the one the native modules were built for. That turns a silent mismatch into a clear error in the log.

**Placement.** The `.pkg` installs to `/usr/local/bin`, which would compete with `/opt/homebrew/bin` on your PATH. If you keep Homebrew's node for dev, the official **tarball** extracted to a versioned folder (say `~/.local/node/v26.13.1/`) is cleaner: only the plist points at it, and a version switch means editing one path. I'm less sure the tarball binary is signed the same way as the `.pkg`, so check `codesign -dv` before relying on grants surviving upgrades.

**My pick:** option 2 with the tarball, plus the guard rail. Prod gets its own checkout, its own node, and its own `node_modules`, and Homebrew can't touch any of it. Want me to file that as a decision bead for you to look over?

Project learnings have three distinct destinations. Confusing them is the main
failure mode: the same fact in the wrong home is either invisible (never read
at the right moment) or noise (read when it doesn't apply).

| Home | Character | What belongs there |
|---|---|---|
| **`.claude/REFLECTIONS.md`** (project, local, gitignored) | *Reflective* — how we understand the project | Mental models, insights, gotchas-with-context, why decisions went the way they did, approaches that failed and why, open questions still being mulled |
| **`CLAUDE.md`** (project) | *Instructive* — rules to follow | Commands, conventions, constraints, "do X / never Y" |
| **Beads** (`bd`), if the project has it | *Backlog* — work to do | Unfinished tasks, next steps, blockers, cross-session work state (`bd` issues / `bd remember`) |

Litmus test: a rule the agent should **obey** → CLAUDE.md. A task someone
should **do** → Beads. Understanding worth **carrying forward** — context,
judgment, hard-won intuition → REFLECTIONS.md. When a learning has both an
instructive and a reflective half (a correction *and* the story behind it),
split it: the rule goes to CLAUDE.md, the why goes to REFLECTIONS.md.

**In Beads projects:** `bd init` generates guidance telling agents to keep
persistent knowledge in `bd remember` rather than memory files. That guidance
is about task memory — work state, handoffs, backlog context — and Beads
remains the right home for all of it. REFLECTIONS.md is not that: it holds
reflective *understanding*, which has no natural home in an issue tracker.
In a Beads project, use both: backlog and work state in `bd`, understanding
in REFLECTIONS.md. The bd guidance does not apply to this file.

Two destinations live outside the project:

- **Durable facts about the user** (role, standing preferences, recurring
  feedback that follows them across repos) → user-level file-based memory, per
  your environment's memory protocol.
- **"From now on / always / whenever X" automations, settings, permissions** →
  the harness must enforce these, not memory. Delegate to the `update-config`
  skill (hooks, env vars, settings) or `fewer-permission-prompts` (allowlists).

## The flow

### 1 — Survey the session

Read back over the conversation and produce a short candidate list — each item
one line, grounded in a real moment. The richest signals:

- The user corrected, redirected, or pushed back → a preference or constraint.
- "From now on / always / every time" → an automation request (→ settings/hook).
- You had to *discover* something that should have been known — a command,
  a convention, where things live, a gotcha → project knowledge.
- You took a wrong turn and course-corrected → capture the root cause and the
  story, not just the symptom.
- Work is unfinished or spans sessions → work state for Beads.
- Something surprised you, or your model of the project meaningfully changed →
  exactly what REFLECTIONS.md exists for.

The bar for keeping a candidate: durable (true beyond this conversation),
generalizable (helps a future session, not a replay of this one), and not
already captured in the repo, CLAUDE.md, REFLECTIONS.md, or git history. Five sharp
candidates beat twenty vague ones; if you can't say why a future session
benefits, drop it. A session-end run that records two real learnings and says "nothing
else worth keeping" is a success — don't manufacture findings.

### 2 — Route each candidate

Use the tables above. Two judgment calls that recur:

- *Project-specific preference* → CLAUDE.md (instructive) or REFLECTIONS.md
  (reflective) by the litmus test. *Preference that follows the user
  everywhere* → user memory. Prefer the narrower scope when torn.
- *"Always do X"* — if the harness can enforce it (run a command, block an
  action, inject context) it's a hook; if it requires judgment or taste it
  belongs in CLAUDE.md or REFLECTIONS.md. A hook can't hold taste.

### 3 — Update `.claude/REFLECTIONS.md`

This file is a **curated living document, not a journal**. Treat every update
as an edit of the whole, not an append:

1. Read the existing file first. If absent, create it with a short header
   explaining what it is. If the session ran in a linked git worktree, the
   file lives in the *primary* worktree's `.claude/` (first entry of
   `git worktree list`) — it's ignored by git, so a copy left in a feature
   worktree dies when that worktree is removed.
2. Integrate: merge new learnings into the section where they belong; refine
   entries this session confirmed, sharpened, or contradicted; prune entries
   that are now stale, resolved, or absorbed into CLAUDE.md/code.
3. Keep it bounded and readable — if it has crept past roughly 150 lines,
   consolidate before adding. A future session should be able to read the
   whole thing cold in a minute.

A workable skeleton (adapt sections to what the project actually needs):

```markdown
# Project Reflections

Reflective notes maintained at session end. Rules live in CLAUDE.md;
backlog lives in Beads. This file is for understanding. Local only —
ignored by git.

## Current understanding
## Lessons & gotchas
## What we tried that didn't work
## Open questions
```

Write entries so they're useful cold: the insight plus enough context that a
reader who wasn't in this session understands *why* it's true. Date an entry
("as of 2026-08") only when recency matters to its validity.

### 4 — Ask only when genuinely unsure; optionally share

Default is autonomous: write the updates, then show the user what changed.
Ask a question only when a learning is genuinely ambiguous, contradicts
something already recorded, or hinges on intent only the user knows. Batch
such questions into one round (at most ~3) rather than dribbling them out.

You may also share one or two brief memories from the session — a moment that
was satisfying, surprising, or instructive. Keep it genuine and short; skip it
entirely if nothing stands out. This is a human touch, not a required section.

### 5 — Apply, with the safe/risky line

Apply **safe** changes as a presented batch; confirm **risky** ones item by item.

- *Safe:* writing/updating REFLECTIONS.md, appending a note to CLAUDE.md (via the
  `claude-md-management:revise-claude-md` skill if available), writing user
  memory + its index pointer, creating Beads issues / a `bd remember` handoff,
  allowlisting a clearly read-only command.
- *Risky:* creating or modifying hooks (they execute automatically), changing
  or removing existing settings or permissions, rewriting existing CLAUDE.md
  content (vs. appending), allowlisting anything that writes or reaches the
  network. When in doubt, it's risky — the cost of asking is one sentence.

Delegate config edits to the specialist skills named in step 2 rather than
hand-editing; they handle placement and dedup. Fall back to careful direct
edits only if a skill isn't available.

### 6 — Git: ignore REFLECTIONS.md, hotfix doc edits straight onto main

Skip this step if the project isn't a git repository.

**REFLECTIONS.md is never committed.** It's a local, per-machine working file,
so updating it should never produce a diff, a commit, or a PR. Make sure git
ignores it:

- If `git check-ignore -q .claude/REFLECTIONS.md` fails, add the line
  `.claude/REFLECTIONS.md` to the repo-root `.gitignore` (this is committed
  on the default branch, below). Also append the same line to
  `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/info/exclude` if it isn't there. A
  feature branch won't see the new `.gitignore` until it picks up main, while
  `info/exclude` applies to every branch and worktree immediately and is
  never itself a change.
- If it's already tracked (`git ls-files --error-unmatch .claude/REFLECTIONS.md`
  succeeds), untrack it with `git rm --cached .claude/REFLECTIONS.md`. This
  keeps the local copy. Mention it in the close-out.

**Everything else session-end changed in tracked files** (CLAUDE.md edits, the
`.gitignore` line, the untracking) **is docs-only, so hotfix it directly on the
default branch and push.** This explicitly bypasses the project's
branch → worktree → PR → CI workflow, even when CLAUDE.md says never to commit
to main. This skill is the user's standing approval for that exception. The
reasoning: session-end is the last thing a session does, and a PR waiting on CI
would strand the edits after `/exit`. Docs-only changes also carry no risk
that CI would catch.

1. Find the default branch (`git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`,
   falling back to `main`/`master`).
2. Commit on the default branch, never on the session's feature branch. The
   session may still be on a feature branch or in a worktree with
   half-finished code, and the doc edits must not ride along with it or touch
   it. If the current checkout isn't on the default branch, make the edits in
   the primary worktree if that one is on the default branch with no staged
   changes. Otherwise use `git worktree add <tmp> <default>` for a temporary
   checkout, then remove it once you've pushed. Don't stash, switch branches
   in, or otherwise disturb the session's own checkout.
3. Stage only the session-end files by explicit path (`git add CLAUDE.md
   .gitignore`, never `-A`/`.`). If anything other than docs would end up in
   the commit, it doesn't qualify for the hotfix exception, so leave it out.
4. Commit as one small commit (e.g. `docs: session-end notes`) with the
   commit trailers your environment requires, then `git pull --rebase` and
   `git push origin <default>`.
5. If there's no remote, the commit alone is enough. If the push is rejected
   (branch protection, auth), don't force it and don't fall back to opening a
   PR. Leave the commit local and report it in the close-out.

A current "don't commit" or "don't push" from the user still wins over all of
this.

### 7 — Close out

End with one compact final message:

- What was written where — one line per destination actually touched,
  including the hotfix commit on the default branch and whether it was pushed.
- Recommendations only the user can act on, if any.
- A one-line handoff: where the next session should look first (REFLECTIONS.md,
  a Beads issue, a branch).
- Then tell the user the session is ready to close — it's safe to `/exit`.

Do not recommend `/compact`, start new work, or leave dangling promises. The
session is over; everything worth keeping is on disk.

## Current understanding

- **Top-level Slack messages already reach the daemon; thread-only scope is a
  choice, not a technical limit.** With `channels:history` + the
  `message.channels` Event Subscription, Slack delivers *every* channel message
  to the `message` handler in `src/slack/inbound-router.ts` — including
  top-level ones that @mention the bot. The router drops them only because they
  lack a `thread_ts`. Consequence: supporting top-level @mentions would **not**
  require the `app_mentions:read` scope / an `app_mention` handler (the natural
  assumption, and the one bd `meal-planner-kqq` was written under). A dedicated
  `app_mention` path would be *cleaner*, but the message event is already in
  hand. We deliberately kept thread-only anyway (SPEC §7; ratified in bd
  `meal-planner-j8b`) because the whole revision loop keys on `thread_ts →
  session row`, so a top-level message has no plan context to act on. Read the
  RUNBOOK's "does nothing, by design" line with this nuance: *by design*, not
  *impossible*.

- **The planner had literal amnesia until 2026-09-27, and it showed.** Dedup
  depends on the Todoist recency read, which failed every week (bd `54i`) and
  whose data source (the v3.0 round-trip, `4sr`) isn't live — so across 7
  weeks of plans the bot used only **17 distinct recipes out of 765**. The fix
  (bd `5uy`, PR #75) treats each week's *initial* posted plan as accepted:
  `session.initial_plan` is written once at suggest and never revised, and
  `plan-memory.ts` unions the last 8 weeks' main dishes with the Todoist read.
  Two design choices worth keeping in mind: (1) *initial*, not latest — the
  user's explicit call, and `working_plan`/`last_posted_plan` both mutate on
  revision, hence the new column; (2) the union catches a Todoist throw
  *itself*, because `buildPlan`'s degrade-silently catch would otherwise
  discard the local memory along with the failed Todoist result.
